title: How would you design a production RAG pipeline end-to-end in 2025-26?
description: Ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector store, hybrid retrieval, rerank, generation and eval — the full 1M-doc RAG architecture.
answer:
**TL;DR:** A production RAG pipeline is ingestion -> chunk -> embed -> store with metadata -> hybrid retrieve (vector + BM25) -> rerank -> stuff+generate with citations -> eval loop. Every stage is observable and versioned.
Modern RAG is not just vector search. In 2025-26 the baseline is **hybrid + rerank** with eval-gated releases: - **Ingest**: parse PDFs/HTML/Slack with structure preservation (LlamaParse/Unstructured), CDC via queue, store `doc_id`, `tenant_id`, `acl`, `updated_at` alongside vectors. - **Chunk/Embed**: see chunking question; use Matryoshka embeddings (3072 -> truncate to 1024/256 without re-embed) and normalize. - **Retrieve**: vector (HNSW) + lexical (BM25/OpenSearch) fused by RRF, filtered by tenant/ACL *before* ANN. - **Rerank**: cross-encoder scores `(query, chunk)` jointly — biggest precision win for +30ms. - **Generate**: stuff top 6 chunks with citations, instruct `answer only from context or say insufficient`, stream, then run guardrails. | Stage | Tooling 2025-26 | Key Knob | Failure if skipped | |---|---|---|---| | Ingest | LlamaParse, Unstructured, Airbyte | chunk parent pointer | garbage chunks = ceiling on recall | | Embed | text-embedding-3-large, bge-m3, Jina v3 | Matryoshka dim, normalization | incompatible dims break search | | Vector DB | pgvector / Pinecone / Qdrant | HNSW m/ef, quantization | latency or recall cliff | | Retrieval | Hybrid RRF | k=40 then rerank | misses on keywords (IDs, errors) | | Rerank | Cohere Rerank 3.5, bge-reranker-v2 | top_n=6 | LLM sees noisy context, hallucinates | | Eval | Ragas, DeepEval | faithfulness >0.85 | silent quality drift | **Interview Tip:** Draw the 5 boxes left-to-right, then say 'I would start eval before optimizing — log retrieval hits and run Ragas faithfulness so we know if misses are retrieval vs generation.' ```typescript // Hybrid retrieve + rerank + generate (pseudo) const candidates = await hybridSearch({ query, filter: { tenantId }, topK: 40 }); // vector + BM25 RRF const reranked = await reranker.rerank(query, candidates, { topN: 6, model: 'rerank-english-v3.5' }); const prompt = buildGroundedPrompt(query, reranked); // citations + 'answer only from context' const stream = await openai.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o-mini', stream: true, messages: [{ role: 'system', content: SYSTEM }, { role: 'user', content: prompt }] }); ```

title: Chunking in RAG: how do you pick size, overlap, and strategy?
description: Fixed window vs semantic vs late chunking — the trade-offs that make or break retrieval recall.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Start 512 tokens / 15-20% overlap with structure-aware splits; small chunks help precision, large chunks help context. Late chunking embeds whole doc then slices.
Chunking decides the upper bound on RAG quality: - **Fixed window** (e.g., RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter 512/80) is the baseline — simple, overlap prevents sentence bisection. - **Structure-aware**: split on `#`/`##`, table boundaries, code fences. Use a markdown/HTML AST so a table row never straddles chunks — critical for financial/legal docs. - **Hierarchical / small-to-big**: embed 256-512 token children, but return their 2k parent when cited — gives precise search + rich context without stuffing many small chunks. - **Late chunking** (Jina AI 2024-25): run transformer over full document with long context, then pool per-chunk. Vectors 'see' surrounding context, boosting recall on anaphora ('it', 'this policy'). | Strategy | Recall | Precision | When to use | |---|---|---|---| | 256 + 10% overlap | high | lower (fragmented) | Q&A on dense manuals, with rerank | | 512 + 20% | balanced | balanced | Default for most knowledge bases | | 1024 + 15% | lower | higher | Narrative docs, contracts | | Semantic / AST | highest for tables | high | Docs with tables/code — keep rows intact | | Late chunking | +5-8% recall | high | Small corpus where quality > indexing cost | **Interview Tip:** Say 'I will eval chunk sizes against our reranker — split a golden set, measure Ragas context precision@k for 256/512/1024, and pick the smallest size that keeps that metric flat.' ```python from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter headers = [('#', 'h1'), ('##', 'h2'), ('###', 'h3')] md_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(headers_to_split_on=headers) sections = md_splitter.split_text(markdown) splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=80, separators=['\n## ', '\n', '. ', ' ']) chunks = splitter.split_documents(sections) # attach parent_id + page + tenant for filtered retrieval ```

title: Embeddings in 2025-26: how do you choose model, dimensions, and distance?
description: text-embedding-3-large vs bge-m3 vs Jina v3, Matryoshka truncation, and cosine vs dot pitfalls.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Use Matryoshka-capable models (text-embedding-3-large, bge-m3, Jina v3) — store 3072d but truncate to 1024/256 at query time without re-embedding. Normalize and use cosine/dot.
- **Model choice 2025**: `text-embedding-3-large` (MRL, 3072), `bge-m3` (multi-lingual + multi-function), `jina-embeddings-v3` (long 8k context) — all MRL/Matryoshka. Benchmark on *your* data, not MTEB alone. - **Matryoshka (MRL)**: train vectors so prefix dims remain meaningful — store full 3072 but query with 1024 for speed or 256 for mobile cache with <2% recall loss. - **Distance**: L2-normalize -> cosine == dot product. If you forget normalization, dot and cosine diverge. - **Multilingual**: bge-m3 handles 100+ languages; text-embedding-3-large is English-strong but weaker on low-resource. | Model | Dims | MRL? | Context | Strength | |---|---|---|---|---| | text-embedding-3-large | 3072 | Yes | 8191 | Best English, MRL, per-token cheaper at 256d | | bge-m3 | 1024 | Yes | 8192 | Multilingual 100+ langs, dense+sparse | | jina-embeddings-v3 | 1024 | Yes | 8192 | Long docs, late chunking | | Cohere embed-v4 | 1024 | Yes | 512 | Rerank synergy, good for QA | **Interview Tip:** 'I would store full dims but create two indexes — 1024d for prod search and 256d for autocomplete — by truncating the same vectors; never mix models between query and docs.' ```typescript import OpenAI from 'openai'; const openai = new OpenAI(); // Store full 3072, truncate at query time const full = await openai.embeddings.create({ model: 'text-embedding-3-large', input: chunk, dimensions: 3072 }); const queryVec = await openai.embeddings.create({ model: 'text-embedding-3-large', input: query, dimensions: 1024 }); const truncatedDoc = full.data[0].embedding.slice(0, 1024); // MRL prefix is valid const norm = (v: number[]) => { const n = Math.hypot(...v); return v.map(x => x/n); }; ```

title: Reranking in RAG: when and how to add a cross-encoder?
description: Bi-encoder recall then cross-encoder precision — Cohere Rerank 3.5 vs bge-reranker trade-offs.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Retrieve 40 with fast bi-encoders, then rerank to 6 with a cross-encoder. It is the cheapest +10-15% nDCG win for RAG.
Bi-encoders embed query and doc separately and compare vectors — fast but shallow. Cross-encoders feed `[query, document]` together through a transformer, letting every query token attend to every doc token — far more accurate, but O(n) per pair so only on 40-100 candidates. - **When**: always for RAG with >10k docs if you care about precision; skip only for <5ms autocomplete. - **Models 2025**: Cohere `rerank-english-v3.5` (hosted, multilingual), `bge-reranker-v2-m3` (self-host, OSS), `jina-reranker-v2`. - **Tuning**: `topN=6`, discard score < 0.3 or `max_tokens` budget, log score distribution to catch drift. | Approach | Latency 40 docs | nDCG@6 gain | Cost | Host | |---|---|---|---|---| | No rerank (bi only) | 0 ms | baseline | $0 | — | | bge-reranker-v2-m3 (GPU) | ~25ms | +9-12% | GPU seconds | self-host | | Cohere Rerank 3.5 (API) | ~35ms | +12-16% | ~$2 / 1k queries | managed | | LLM-as-reranker (GPT-4o) | ~500ms | +15% but pricey | ~$10 / 1k | wasteful | **Interview Tip:** 'I would show the two-stage waterfall and say reranking pays for itself — 40->6 cuts prompt tokens by 6x, so the reranker cost is offset by LLM savings.' ```python import cohere co = cohere.ClientV2(api_key='...') reranked = co.rerank( model='rerank-english-v3.5', query=query, documents=[c['text'] for c in candidates], top_n=6 ) top_chunks = [candidates[r.index] for r in reranked.results if r.relevance_score > 0.3] ```

title: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant: how do you choose a vector DB in 2025?
description: Self-hosted Postgres vs managed ANN — scale, cost, filtering, and tenancy trade-offs.
answer:
**TL;DR:** pgvector for <5M vectors + strong OLTP needs; Pinecone/Qdrant for >10M, heavy filtering, and serverless scale. Do not pick on hype — measure QPS, filter selectivity, and tenancy.
- **pgvector (Postgres)**: lives inside your OLTP, transactional, `JOIN` on `tenant_id`, HNSW + IVFFlat, `pgvector 0.8` supports HNSW iterative scan. Great for <5M, <1k QPS, when you already run Postgres. Watch `maintenance_work_mem` for HNSW build and need `halfvec` for 2k+ dims. - **Pinecone serverless (2024+)**: managed, 10-100M+, sparse+dense hybrid, metadata filtering, autoscale, separate storage/compute pricing — zero ops but egress + per-write cost. - **Qdrant / Weaviate / Milvus**: self-host or cloud, best filtering and payload handling, quantization (SQ/PQ), multi-tenancy via collections/partitions. | Criteria | pgvector | Pinecone Serverless | Qdrant Cloud | |---|---|---|---| | Vectors | <5M sweet spot | 10M-1B | 5M-100M | | Latency p95 1k QPS | ~40-90ms (needs tuning) | ~20-40ms | ~20-50ms | | Filtering | SQL WHERE (pre-filter) | metadata + sparse | payload index + pre-filter | | Tenancy | row-level ACL, RLS | namespaces | collections + shards | | Ops | you own Postgres | fully managed | half-managed | | Cost model | compute you already pay | per read/write + storage | per node + storage | **Interview Tip:** Answer with numbers: 'For 2M docs, 300 QPS, need ACL joins -> pgvector saves a system. For 20M with 30% filtered queries -> dedicated DB; I would load-test 5k filtered QPS before committing.' ```sql -- pgvector HNSW with tenant filter (pre-filter via WHERE) CREATE INDEX ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m=16, ef_construction=200); SELECT id, text, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS score FROM docs WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND acl @> ARRAY[$3] ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 6; ``` ```typescript // Pinecone equivalent await index.namespace(tenantId).query({ vector: queryVec, topK: 6, filter: { acl: userId } }); ```

title: Hybrid search: why combine BM25 with vectors and how does RRF work?
description: Lexical + semantic fusion via Reciprocal Rank Fusion — covering keyword and meaning gaps.
answer:
**TL;DR:** BM25 catches exact keywords/IDs vectors miss; vectors catch paraphrase BM25 misses. Run both, fuse with RRF (1/(k+rank)).
Vectors understand meaning but embed rare tokens (SKUs, error codes, names) poorly. BM25 nails exact matches but not 'how do I get my money back' == 'refund policy'. Hybrid runs both: - Query both in parallel (vector top 40, BM25 top 40). - Fuse with **RRF**: `score(d) = sum 1/(k + rank_i(d))` where k=60 dampens top-rank dominance. No score normalization needed unlike weighted sums. - Deduplicate by id, keep top 40, then rerank. | Fusion | Needs score norm | Handles scale skew | Default k | When | |---|---|---|---|---| | RRF | No | Yes | 60 | Default — robust | | Weighted sum (0.7 dense) | Yes (min-max) | No | — | When you tuned alpha on eval | | Convex + alpha | Yes | No | alpha 0.5-0.8 | Needs per-domain tuning | **Interview Tip:** If asked 'vector only?', say 'It fails on exact IDs — hybrid is the default in 2025; I would show RRF formula and note we log per-source recall to tune alpha if we later move to weighted sum.' ```python # RRF fusion (pseudo) def rrf(rank_lists, k=60): scores = {} for lst in rank_lists: for rank, doc_id in enumerate(lst, 1): scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0) + 1/(k + rank) return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)[:40] # Pinecone hybrid (dense + sparse) or pgvector + OpenSearch vec_ids = vector_search(query_vec, 40) bm25_ids = opensearch.search(query, 40) fused = rrf([vec_ids, bm25_ids]) ```

title: Evaluating RAG with Ragas: faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision?
description: The 4 Ragas metrics that gate RAG releases — how to compute and what breaks them.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Ragas scores RAG without human labels: faithfulness (grounded?), answer relevancy (on point?), context precision/recall (retrieved right docs?). Gate releases on them.
Ragas (0.2.x, 2025) is LLM-as-judge for RAG: - **Faithfulness**: splits answer into claims, checks each claim is entailed by contexts — low means hallucination. - **Answer Relevancy**: reverse — generate questions from answer, compare to original. - **Context Precision**: are top retrieved contexts relevant (precision@k via judge). - **Context Recall**: does retrieval contain GT answer (needs labeled dataset). - **Context Utilization**: newer. Run on 200-500 golden Q&A (synthetic + human-labeled). Use `gpt-4o-mini` as judge for cost, `gpt-4o` for final gate. | Metric | Needs GT | What it tells you | Fix when low | |---|---|---|---| | Faithfulness | No | hallucinating? | stricter grounding prompt, fewer chunks | | Answer Relevancy | No | off-topic? | better query rewriting | | Context Precision | No (judge) | noisy retrieval | add rerank, lower k | | Context Recall | Yes | missing docs | larger k, hybrid, chunk fix | **Interview Tip:** 'I would run Ragas in CI on every prompt/chunk change and show the 4-number delta — if faithfulness drops but recall is flat, the generator regressed, not retriever.' ```python from ragas import evaluate from ragas.metrics import faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall from datasets import Dataset ds = Dataset.from_list([{ 'question': 'What is refund window?', 'contexts': ['Refund within 30 days...'], 'answer': '30 days.', 'ground_truth': '30 days' }]) results = evaluate(ds, metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall]) print(results) # {'faithfulness': 0.92, 'context_precision': 0.88, ...} # Gate: fail CI if faithfulness < 0.85 ```

title: Beyond Ragas: how do you eval LLMs with LLM-as-judge, DeepEval, and human eval?
description: Designing a balanced eval harness — rubric, bias mitigation, and eval-to-prod loop.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Combine deterministic checks (exact/regex) + LLM judge (rubric-anchored) + sampled human audit. DeepEval/Braintrust run it in CI with versioned prompts.
- **Dataset**: 200-500 cases covering happy path, edge, adversarial. Include `expected` + rubric. Version with prompt in same commit. - **Grader layers**: (1) code — schema, regex, function call valid; (2) LLM judge — rubric-anchored Likert with `references` and `reason` fields. Use `gpt-4o` or `claude-3.5` as judge (different family than generator to reduce bias). - **Bias fixes**: position bias (shuffle A/B), length bias (rubric says brevity rewarded), self-preference (judge != generator), temperature 0. - **Tooling**: DeepEval (`GEval`), Braintrust, LangSmith, Evidently. Store traces -> auto-build eval set from prod failures. | Grader | Cost | Signal | Pitfall | |---|---|---|---| | Exact/regex | $0 | format, IDs | misses semantic | | LLM judge (rubric) | ~$0.01/case | relevance, faithfulness | bias, judge drift | | Embedding similarity | $0 | paraphrase | weak on logic | | Human (5% sample) | $$$ | ground truth | slow, needs calibration | **Interview Tip:** 'I would describe the eval pyramid — 80% deterministic, 15% LLM judge with bias mitigations, 5% human — and say we calibrate the judge quarterly by measuring correlation with human scores.' ```python # DeepEval GEval example from deepeval.metrics import GEval from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase, LLMTestCaseParams correctness = GEval( name='Correctness', criteria='Does answer match ground truth and cite context? Score 0-5, 5=perfect.', params=[LLMTestCaseParams.ACTUAL_OUTPUT, LLMTestCaseParams.EXPECTED_OUTPUT, LLMTestCaseParams.CONTEXT], ) test_case = LLMTestCase(input='Refund window?', actual_output='30 days', expected_output='30 days', context=['Refund within 30 days']) print(correctness.measure(test_case)) # score + reason ```

title: Prompt caching in 2025: how do you cut cost with Anthropic & OpenAI caches?
description: KV-cache reuse for static prefixes — cache keys, TTL, and 90% token discounts.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Put static prefix (system, few-shot, large context) first. Anthropic needs explicit cache_control breakpoints (5m TTL, 90% off cached reads); OpenAI caches automatically. Hit rate is everything.
- **Anthropic (Claude 3.5/4, 2025)**: add `cache_control: {type:'ephemeral'}` on prefix blocks. Minimum 1024 tokens, last `cache_control` is evicted first. 4 breakpoints max, 5m TTL (or 1h beta). Writes cost ~1.25x, reads 0.1x. - **OpenAI (2024-25)**: automatic prompt caching for prompts >1024 tokens that share prefix — no code change, 50% discount on cached input after ~128 tokens. API returns `usage.cached_tokens`. - **Design**: sort prompts stable-first: system -> tools -> few-shot -> large static doc -> user query last. Keep prefix byte-identical (no timestamp inside prefix!). Cache `system` + `retrieved context` across turns in chat. | Provider | API | Discount | TTL | Min tokens | |---|---|---|---|---| | Anthropic Claude | `cache_control` breakpoints | 90% off read, 1.25x write | 5m (1h beta) | 1024 | | OpenAI GPT-4o | automatic (no param) | 50% off cached | minutes, auto | ~1024 | | Google Gemini | `cachedContent` explicit | ~75% off | 1h | 32k | | Vercel AI SDK | `experimental_cache` | inherited | — | — | **Interview Tip:** 'I would diagram the prefix/suffix split and say we moved timestamps and user query to the suffix, raising cache hit from 20% to 82% and cutting TTFT by 40%.' ```typescript // Anthropic prompt caching (explicit) const msg = await anthropic.messages.create({ model: 'claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022', max_tokens: 1024, system: [{ type: 'text', text: SYSTEM, cache_control: { type: 'ephemeral' } }], // cached messages: [ { role: 'user', content: [{ type: 'text', text: largeContext, cache_control: { type: 'ephemeral' } }] }, { role: 'user', content: query } // suffix — not cached, varies ] }); // OpenAI — same prefix automatically cached; check usage const out = await openai.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o-mini', messages: [SYSTEM, ...fewShot, { role:'user', content: query }] }); console.log(out.usage?.prompt_tokens_details?.cached_tokens); ```

title: Fine-tune vs RAG vs prompt engineering: how do you choose in 2025-26?
description: Cost, freshness, and style — the decision tree and when to combine.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Prompt+RAG for knowledge (fresh, cited); fine-tune for style/format/tool-use; prompt engineering first. Cost order: prompt < RAG < LoRA < full FT.
- **Prompt engineering**: fastest, cheapest, no training data. Good for instructions, few-shot style. Fails when context >32k or needs proprietary style at scale. - **RAG**: knowledge is fresh (re-index), auditable (citations), multi-tenant via filters. Fails when task is behavior/format that retrieval cannot teach. - **LoRA/PEFT** (2025 default): train 1-10k pairs for tone, tool-call schema compliance, classification. Cheap on 1xA100, base model frozen. - **Full fine-tune / DPO**: rare in 2025-26 (use for reasoning/style distillation). Expensive, needs eval + safeguards against forgetting. | Need | Answer | Why | |---|---|---| | Facts change weekly | RAG | no retrain | | Cite sources | RAG | grounding | | Consistent voice/format | LoRA FT | prompt too brittle | | Tool-call accuracy >95% | LoRA on traces | prompt misses edge | | Latency + tiny model | Distill FT | RAG adds hops | **Interview Tip:** 'I would say we fine-tune for *form*, RAG for *facts* — show a 2x2 of freshness vs style and note most 2025 teams ship RAG first, add LoRA only after prompt+RAG plateaus on eval.' ```python # LoRA with HuggingFace PEFT (or OpenAI FT) from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=['q_proj','v_proj'], lora_dropout=0.05, task_type='CAUSAL_LM') model = get_peft_model(base_model, config) # train on {"messages":[{"role":"user","content":...},{"role":"assistant","content":...,"tool_calls":...}]} # OpenAI fine-tune (managed) # openai fine_tuning.jobs.create({training_file: fileId, model: 'gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18', suffix: 'support-style'}) ```

title: Cost optimization for LLM apps: how do you keep the bill predictable?
description: Token math, caching, model routing, and observability for AI spend.
answer:
**TL;DR:** Cost = tokens x price + calls. Cut with prompt caching, smaller routed models, truncated contexts, batch for async, and per-feature metering.
Math: `cost = sum(input_tokens * price_in + output_tokens * price_out)` — output ~3-5x input price, so cap max tokens and encourage concise answers. Levers ranked by impact 2025: 1) **Prompt caching** (see prior) — biggest quick win for RAG chat. 2) **Model routing** — classify `easy/medium/hard` with a 0.5ms DistilBERT, route 70% traffic to `haiku/mini`. 3) **Context shrink** — rerank to 6 docs, truncate embeddings, summarize history. 4) **Batch API** — OpenAI `Batch` is 50% off for non-urgent (evals, ingest). 5) **Semantic cache** — cache LLM answers by embedding similarity (threshold 0.96) for FAQ. | Lever | Saving | Latency | Risk | |---|---|---|---| | Prompt cache | 40-80% input | -TTFT | prefix must be stable | | Model router | 50-70% blended | lower p95 | misroute -> quality drop | | Rerank 40->6 | 60% prompt tokens | +30ms | bad rerank hurts recall | | Batch API | 50% | async (24h SLA) | not for realtime | | Semantic cache | 20-40% calls | -latency | false hit if threshold low | **Interview Tip:** 'I would write cost = tokens x price on board, then stack the 5 levers and say we meter per-feature via OTEL `gen_ai.usage` so we can attribute $ to product, not just global bill.' ```typescript // Router + metering (pseudo) import { generateText } from 'ai'; import { openai, anthropic } from './models'; const tier = await classify(query); // 'easy' | 'hard' const model = tier === 'easy' ? openai('gpt-4o-mini') : anthropic('claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022'); const result = await generateText({ model, prompt: query, maxTokens: 512 }); await meter.record({ feature: 'chat', model: result.modelId, in: result.usage.inputTokens, out: result.usage.outputTokens }); // Batch for async eval (50% off) await openai.batches.create({ input_file_id: fileId, endpoint: '/v1/chat/completions', completion_window: '24h' }); ```

title: Context windows in 2025-26: how do you use 128k-1M tokens without drowning?
description: Lost-in-the-middle, needle-in-haystack, and strategies for huge contexts.
answer:
**TL;DR:** 128k is table stakes, Gemini/Claude offer 1M. Do not stuff — retrieve + place key info at start/end, compress middle, and test needle recall.
Providers 2025-26: GPT-4o 128k, Claude 3.5/4 200k, Gemini 1.5/2.0 1-2M. But **needle-in-haystack** tests show recall drops when answer sits in the middle of a huge dump. Best practice: - Retrieve then stuff: RAG top 6 at top, not 200 docs. - If you must pass huge doc (contract), place the question *both* before and after the doc, and ask model to cite page. - Compress: map-reduce summarization or `contextual compression` (LLM extracts relevant sentences before stuffing). | Window | Cheap way | Expensive way | Pitfall | |---|---|---|---| | 8-32k | single call | — | fits most chats | | 128k | prompt cached | uncached $0.15/1M input | stuffing 100 docs | | 1M | Gemini Flash cached | uncached $0.35/1M + TTFT 4s | lost-in-middle | **Interview Tip:** 'I would say 1M != free lunch — I would show lost-in-middle chart and argue we retrieve to 6 docs then place them at edges, using 1M only for single-document reasoning like contracts.' ```typescript // Long-context anti-pattern vs good pattern // Bad: stuff 200 chunks into 128k (model ignores middle) const badPrompt = chunks.slice(0, 200).join('\n---\n'); // Good: RAG top 6 at edges + summarize overflow const top = await rerank(query, chunks, 6); const summary = await summarize(chunks.slice(6, 50)); // map-reduce const prompt = `Question: ${query}\n\nRelevant excerpts (cite id):\n${top.join('\n')}\n\nBackground summary:\n${summary}\n\nQuestion again: ${query}`; ```

title: Guardrails for AI agents: rate limits, budget caps, and HITL?
description: Preventing runaway tool loops, spend, and unsafe side effects in agents.
